message.content:
I don’t have real‑time access to live air‑quality feeds, so I can’t tell you the exact AQI for Los Angeles at this moment.  

**What you can do instead**

| Source | How to use it | Typical data you’ll see |
|--------|---------------|------------------------|
| **AirNow** (U.S. EPA) | Visit <https://www.airnow.gov/> and enter “Los Angeles” or use the mobile app. | Current AQI (0–500), pollutant breakdown (PM₂.₅, O₃, NO₂, etc.), health advice. |
| **AQICN** (World Air Quality Index) | Go to <https://aqicn.org/city/los-angeles/> or use the app. | Real‑time AQI, forecast for the next 24 h, historical trends. |
| **Local news/weather sites** | Many local stations (e.g., KABC, KNBC) publish live air‑quality dashboards. | Often show a color‑coded map and brief health notes. |

**Typical pattern in Los Angeles**

- **Spring & early summer**: Ozone levels often rise, especially on sunny days, leading to “moderate” (AQI 51–100) or sometimes “unhealthy for sensitive groups” (AQI 101–150) readings.
- **Fall & winter**: Particulate matter (PM₂.₅) can spike from wild‑fire smoke or vehicle emissions, sometimes reaching “unhealthy” (AQI 151–200) or higher.
- **Weekends**: Traffic‑related PM₂.₅ can be higher, but ozone may be lower due to reduced traffic.

If you’re planning outdoor activities or have respiratory concerns, it’s best to check one of the above sources right before you head out. Let me know if you’d like help interpreting the numbers or setting up a quick alert!
